en: Now besides the Single Responsibility
Principle, there is one other core principle
you should be aware of when working with
classes, especially in the context of clean
code.
And that's the Open-Closed Principle.
The Open-Closed Principle says that a class
should be open for extension but closed for
modification.
Now what does this mean?
Here is an example. Now again, it's just a
dummy class without actual code because
again, it is more about the general
architecture of your classes, the API of
your classes.
And what we can see is that we have a
Printer class
which actually has different methods for
printing PDF documents, web documents, so
probably HTML pages, and also printPage
which maybe prints real pages in the real
world.
We also have a verifyData method which
probably is called internally to verify the
data from any of these print methods here.
Now what's the problem with this class?
It basically needs to grow whenever we add
new functionality.
If we also want to print Word documents or
Microsoft Excel spreadsheets, we need to add
a new method.
Whenever we need to call a new method
besides verifyData from our print methods,
we have to add that logic to all the print
methods.
So this Printer class might have one
responsibility. It's about printing data and
about generating output,
but it actually is not closed for
modification.
We need to go back to it all the time
whenever we add new functionality. It's not
very extensible.
And therefore it violates the Open-Closed
Principle because it should be closed for
modification, which this one isn't.
Now this might remind you of this

classes for delivering goods

Indeed, the Open-Closed Principle is kind of
related to that.
Instead of having this Printer class here,
it would be preferable to have code like
this,
to have, for example, a Printer interface
and then a base class
which just has this verifyData method which
probably is shared amongst all classes.
But then all these specific subclasses
implement this Printer interface which
forces them to have a print method
and they extend the base class to then all
have a print method
which then just does different things
depending on which class it is.
The advantage is that the base class, the
printer implementation, can be closed for
modification at some point.
Once the API is finished, we close it.
Of course, we can still edit it if we need
to fix bugs, but we don't need to edit it
all the time just to add new features.
Instead, to add new features, we extend it.
And that of course is what the Open-Closed
Principle says. A class should be open for
extension.
And we can build brand new Printer
subclasses like for example a Word or an
ExcelPrinter which just extends the
PrinterImplementation class and implements

This is how we can follow the Open-Closed
Principle.
Now, why does the Open-Closed Principle help
us with clean code?
Or why does it help us with clean code more
than maybe some other principles?
Because this extensibility ensures small
classes
automatically because otherwise, if we don't
extend,
if we stick to the big do-it-all class
instead, then this class, this Printer class
keeps on growing and growing the more ways
of printing we add.
On the other hand, if we have multiple
smaller classes, we can add more and more
features without getting growing and growing
classes.
So it helps us with smaller focused classes
and it can help prevent code duplication. It
can help us stay DRY,
don't repeat yourself. The Open-Closed
Principle helps us with that as well.

because that helps us with
